passage: My name is Sharmila. Last winter my friend Noor said over chai, "I've let go of him, honestly. I'm fine." Her voice was bright and quick, and in the same breath she asked about my sister's wedding. I nodded. But when I mentioned the café where they used to meet, her jaw tightened and she checked her phone twice. Later, when someone joked about exes, she left the room to take a call that nobody had made. I had always thought letting go would look calm. Noor looked like a person holding a door shut with her shoulder. I didn't argue. A week later I said, "When you want to talk about it, or not, I'm here either way." She looked at the floor and said, "Okay. Maybe soon." I still don't know what she felt, but I stopped calling it peace.

qa.q: What did Noor say over chai?
qa.a: Noor said, "I've let go of him, honestly. I'm fine."

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when Noor left the room to take a call nobody had made?
qa.a: Worried and unsure. Sharmila had expected letting go to look calm, and Noor looked tense, so Sharmila stopped calling it peace.

qa.q: What did Sharmila choose to say instead of arguing that Noor had not let go?
qa.a: Sharmila offered to be there whenever Noor wanted to talk, or not, which left room without pushing.

qa.q: How might Noor feel hearing "I'm here either way"?
qa.a: Noor may feel relieved and less pressured, which fits the quiet "Okay. Maybe soon." It is a cue, not proof of what Noor feels.

grounding: A friend hears 'I have let go' from someone who is still tense and avoiding the topic, and does not mistake that for calm.

passage:
Note, Friday. Vikas, team lead.
Sudha, a friend since our first jobs, told me at lunch, "I've let go of the promotion thing. Totally over it." She said it fast, then asked whether I had seen the new cafeteria menu. Since then I have noticed a few things. She skips any meeting where the new manager presents. Her replies to his emails are one word long. Yesterday when a colleague congratulated him, she went very quiet and stacked the same three folders twice. On days when Sudha really is calm, she laughs and mentions such things herself.
What I did: I did not press. I said, "Whenever you want to talk about it, I'll make the tea." She said thanks, tightly.
Next: check in again next week. If the tension keeps going, I will mention the counsellor.

qa.q: What did Sudha say at lunch?
qa.a: "I've let go of the promotion thing. Totally over it."

qa.q: What was Vikas worried about after watching Sudha stack the same folders twice?
qa.a: Vikas worried that Sudha was still hurting and avoiding the subject rather than being at peace.

qa.q: What did Vikas choose to do instead of pressing Sudha to talk?
qa.a: Vikas offered tea whenever Sudha wanted to talk, and planned to check in next week and mention the counsellor if the tension keeps going.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when Vikas says "I'll make the tea"?
qa.a: Sudha may feel cared for but still guarded; the tight thanks suggests Sudha is not ready to talk yet.

passage:
Thursday.
Tejas keeps saying he's let go of Pallavi. "It's done, I'm totally over it, I've moved on." He said it three times at dinner tonight.
But when Kavya mentioned she'd seen Pallavi at the mall, Tejas put his fork down so hard it clattered. He said, "Can we not?" and went to his room. Last week he left the terrace party the moment her song came on.
I don't think I know what's going on inside him. But the "let go" doesn't look peaceful. It looks like he's holding his breath.
When my Nani let go of the old house, she talked about it easily, even laughed about the leaking roof. That was calm. This is not.
I'm not going to push him. But tomorrow I'll ask him to go for a walk and just see if he wants to talk.
Mohit

qa.q: What did Tejas say three times at dinner?
qa.a: That it's done, he's totally over it, and he's moved on.

qa.q: What does Mohit seem to feel about Tejas saying he has let go?
qa.a: Mohit seems doubtful and quietly concerned, sensing that Tejas is avoiding the hurt rather than at peace with it.

qa.q: What small step does Mohit plan, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Asking Tejas for a walk without pushing gives him a calm, low-pressure chance to talk if he wants.

qa.q: How might Tejas be feeling underneath the words?
qa.a: He may still be hurt and tense, since Pallavi's name or song makes him leave or snap.

passage: In their village near Mandya, Raghav noticed Saurabh had stopped going to the temple fair. "I've let go of the land thing with my cousin," Saurabh said whenever anyone asked. "It's finished. I don't think about it." But when the cousin's tractor passed on the road, Saurabh's jaw went tight and he turned his back. At the tea stall, if someone said the cousin's name, Saurabh left his tea half-full. Raghav couldn't be sure what was inside his friend. But he remembered his grandfather, who had truly let go of a quarrel with a neighbour: he greeted the man at weddings, calm, even joking. Saurabh's "letting go" looked nothing like that. One evening Raghav walked with him along the canal. "You don't have to be over it," he said. "It's okay if it still hurts." Saurabh was quiet, then said, "It hurts every day."

qa.q: Where did Saurabh stop going?
qa.a: To the temple fair.

qa.q: What did Raghav feel as he watched Saurabh turn his back on the tractor?
qa.a: Raghav felt concerned and uncertain, sensing that Saurabh's tight jaw showed hurt still pressing on him, not peace.

qa.q: What did Raghav say that helped, and why?
qa.a: He said Saurabh didn't have to be over it and that it was okay if it still hurt, which let Saurabh stop pretending and be honest.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt saying 'It hurts every day'?
qa.a: He probably felt exposed but also relieved to finally admit the ongoing hurt to someone.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing that someone claiming to have let go of a quarrel is still tense and avoiding it, unlike real, peaceful letting go.

passage: At the café near the Cairo metro stop, Nour stirred her coffee too fast. "I've let go of Karim completely," she told Mina. "Honestly. It's done." Mina nodded, but she noticed things. Nour looked away sharply when the couple at the next table started watching wedding videos. She changed the subject twice when Mina mentioned the old study group, where Karim still went. And when the waiter asked, by chance, whether she wanted "the usual, like last time", Nour snapped at him, then apologised, red-faced. Mina remembered her own breakup two years ago. Letting go, when it finally came, had felt quiet, like putting down a heavy bag. This did not look quiet. She reached across the table. "You don't have to be done yet, you know." Nour's eyes filled.

qa.q: What did Nour do when the couple at the next table started watching wedding videos?
qa.a: She looked away sharply.

qa.q: What was Mina thinking as she noticed Nour's reactions?
qa.a: Mina felt concerned, sensing that Nour's "letting go" was really tense avoidance, unlike the quiet peace Mina had felt after her own breakup.

qa.q: Why was "You don't have to be done yet" a kind thing to say?
qa.a: It gave Nour permission to still hurt instead of pretending, which is where real letting go can begin.

qa.q: How might Nour feel when Mina says this?
qa.a: She probably feels exposed but relieved, which is why her eyes filled.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing that someone who claims to have let go is still hurting and avoiding, tense rather than at peace.
